title: On the Ban Tree a Turtledove Coos
intro: A love poem of forty-four lines from the diwan of al-Malik al-Amjad, the Ayyubid lord of Baalbek; the diwan gives no occasion for it, and its editor notes that all five manuscripts contain it. It opens at night with a turtledove cooing on a ban tree, which sets the poet weeping at the ruins of neighbours who left al-Khayf by night without a farewell, until a flash of lightning recalls Su'da's mouth. It then rides out on camels worn thin by the road, driven by longing towards al-Hima and Hajir, reproaches Su'ad for her betrayal, mourns the grey hair that has left him no one to plead for him, and ends content with mere nearness, kept awake by memories of union. The editor calls al-Amjad's verse “full of rare words”, and this poem bears him out with words like waja, yarma' and mahya'; it also plays again and again on words of one root or sound, such as barq and burqu', jiz' and ajza'.

translation: On the ban tree a turtledove is cooing,
and the robe of darkness hangs down, dusky black.
1.sharh: A turtledove coos on a ban tree in the dead of night, while darkness hangs over everything like a dark robe let down. The dove's cooing is what sets off his grief in the next line.

translation: She sang, and down they poured, having renewed
my passion at the ruined camp: my tears.
2.sharh: The dove sang, and at the ruined camp his tears poured down, reviving a love that had lain quiet. The subject of “poured” and “renewed” is “the tears”, which the Arabic holds back to the very end; “renewed” may also have the dove as its subject.

translation: By it I recalled neighbours who struck their tents
and left al-Khayf by night, with no farewell.
3.sharh: The ruin brought back neighbours who had camped at al-Khayf, then struck their tents and left by night without a farewell. Leaving by night meant he never had a last look at them.

translation: I rained my tears upon their spring camp
till the camp itself all but softened towards me.
4.sharh: He wept over their spring camp until his tears fell on it like rain, and the empty camp itself almost took pity on him. Rain revives a camping ground; here his tears play the rain.

translation: An eye that parts from those it loves
and those it lives among: how could it not weep?
5.sharh: He excuses his tears: an eye parted from those it loves and has lived among cannot help weeping. The Arabic asks the question in a way that allows no other answer.

translation: Once they had gone, I complained to the house
of the hurt of parting, if only it could hear.
6.sharh: Once they had gone he poured out to their empty house the pain of parting, knowing it could not hear. “If only it could hear” leaves unsaid what it would do: pity him.

translation: But complaining to a blackened trace did no good,
a trace whose bare, empty marks stir me up.
7.sharh: Complaining to the blackened traces of a camp did no good, though their bare marks stir up his grief each time he sees them. The ruin cannot answer him, yet it can still hurt him.

translation: How could I be seen glad, now that
the dwellings are empty of their fawns?
8.sharh: No one will see him glad now that the dwellings have lost the young women who lived there. He calls them “fawns”, the young of wild cattle, as if the camp had been a pasture where they grazed.

translation: The wind has wiped away its traces,
but the wind of my passion for it is a gale.
9.sharh: The wind has wiped out the traces of the camp, but another wind blows inside him, his passion for it, and that one is a gale. One wind erases and the other keeps love alive, and the poet calls both by the same word, rih.

translation: Passion is nothing but a breast that flutters
and a heart in pain at their parting,
10.sharh: Passion, he says, is nothing but a breast that flutters and a heart that aches at their parting. He defines love by what it does to the body, and the definition runs on through the next two lines.

translation: and the fire of parting, over whose heat
my ribs close because they have gone,
11.sharh: Passion is also the fire of parting, shut in behind his ribs so that its heat cannot escape. “Fire” continues the list that began with “a breast that flutters” in the line before.

translation: and an eye that, once it sees a lightning cloud,
neither runs dry nor sleeps.
12.sharh: Passion is also an eye that, once it sees lightning in a cloud, neither stops weeping nor sleeps. Why lightning has that power, the next two lines explain.

translation: The lightning stirred my longing when it showed,
its flashes gleaming through the dark,
13.sharh: The lightning stirred his longing when it showed, its flashes gleaming through the dark. The night of the opening line returns, now lit for an instant by something that reminds him of her.

translation: and brought back Su'da's mouth,
the moment the veil slipped from its gleam.
14.sharh: The lightning reminded him of Su'da's mouth at the moment her veil slipped and the white of her teeth flashed. The Arabic sets barq, “flash”, beside burqu', “veil”, two words that sound almost alike.

translation: It made me drink my tears by the cupful,
with the sandy ridge lying between her and me.
15.sharh: The lightning made him swallow his own tears cup after cup, for the sandy ridge lay between him and her. Jarra'ani, “made me swallow”, and al-ajra', “the ridge”, come from the same root.

translation: Many a night, after she left
the bend of the valley, I lay grieving at her going.
16.sharh: Many a night he lay grieving at her departure once she had left the turn of the valley. Al-jiz', “the bend”, echoes ajza', “I grieve”: the place she left names his grief.

translation: But for my love of her, the limping camels
would never have sped me to her.
17.sharh: Only his love for her made the camels hurry him towards her, limping though they were from the long road. Here the poem turns from the ruined camp to the journey.

translation: They jostle on, bridled, through the empty waste,
and their forelegs measure out the long road.
18.sharh: Bridled, the camels press on through the open waste, and their forelegs measure out the long way as cloth is measured by the forearm. The verb “measure” and the noun “forelegs” share a root in Arabic.

translation: Weary, they swoop towards her people,
though they have missed both pasture and water,
19.sharh: Worn out, the camels still swoop towards her people's camp, though the journey has left them no time to graze or drink. Like their rider, they let nothing hold them back.

translation: necks stretched low; we outpace the sandgrouse whenever
I press them, or La'la' comes into view.
20.sharh: Necks stretched low, the camels carry the riders faster than sandgrouse whenever he presses them, or when La'la' comes into view. The sight of a landmark on the road spurs them as much as his urging does, as if they knew where they were going.

translation: But for my love, her sore feet and the white stones
would have kept her from her long stride.
21.sharh: But for his love, her aching feet and the stony ground would have held the camel back from her long stride. His longing drives her on through the pain.

translation: Longing pulls me towards al-Hima;
I urge her on, and she strains on with me.
22.sharh: Longing tugs him towards al-Hima; he urges his camel on, and she too strains towards it, as if his longing had passed into her. The word for “strain” is the one used of a heart drawn to what it loves.

translation: And when the riders go over talk of love,
she travels through the night, the road wide for her.
23.sharh: When the riders keep talking of love, the camel travels on through the night as if the road had opened wide for her. Love talk lightens her way as it lightens his.

translation: So they reach the hills of Hajir worn thin,
carrying us, spent, their heads bowed.
24.sharh: So the camels reach the hills of Hajir, wasted by the road, carrying their riders, their own heads bowed in exhaustion. Hajir is where the journey ends, and they arrive with nothing left.

translation: I cross the darkness and its terrors,
and when I cross it, my resolve is my armour.
25.sharh: He crosses the darkness and all its terrors, and when he does, his resolve is the only armour he needs. “It” in the second half is the darkness.

translation: I seek Su'ad, and my heart is in love with her,
whether she comes near or goes far.
26.sharh: He seeks Su'ad, and his heart is in love with her whether she is near or far: distance does not cool it, nearness does not satisfy it. In line 14 he called her Su'da.

translation: She has betrayed me, though I never betrayed her;
how wretched is what she does now.
27.sharh: She has betrayed him, though he never betrayed her, and he condemns what she has become. The complaint about parting turns here into a reproach: she did not just leave, she broke faith.

translation: Treachery has always been the way of the treacherous:
keep faith with them and they throw it away.
28.sharh: Treachery has always been the way of the treacherous: keep faith with them and they throw it away. He turns her betrayal into a law of human nature.

translation: Is there anyone to plead for me to come near her?
Is there any way back for a union now past?
29.sharh: He longs for someone to plead for him and bring him close to her, and for their old union to come back. The questions are wishes; the next line answers them.

translation: After grey hair, should I look for one to plead for me?
Far from it: what used to plead is gone.
30.sharh: Grey as he is, he scolds himself for looking for someone to plead for him: the one who used to plead for him is gone for good. Line 32 names it: his youth.

translation: Nothing is left but whiteness, which offends
the eyes of the beauties and does no good.
31.sharh: All he has left is white hair, which displeases the eyes of beautiful women and does nothing for him. Where his youth once pleaded for him, his grey hair now turns them away.

translation: A young man's youth stands guard against his being left:
when they mean to leave him, it holds them back.
32.sharh: A man's youth guards him against being dropped: when women want to leave him, it holds them back. This is the advocate he said two lines earlier was gone for good.

translation: May God bring those we love near,
though they shun us, though they resolve to go.
33.sharh: He prays that God bring the ones he loves near, though they shun him and are set on leaving. He answers their coldness with a blessing rather than coldness of his own.

translation: For there is rest in being near the ones I love,
though there is nothing to hope for from them.
34.sharh: Simply being near the ones he loves is a comfort, even with nothing to hope for from them. Having given up on union, he asks only for nearness.

translation: I have settled, willingly, for being near them;
being near their home is enough.
35.sharh: He has settled, willingly, for being near them; living close to where they live is enough for him. Qana'tu, “I have settled”, and maqna', “enough”, come from the same root.

translation: Life is nothing but homes close together,
when what is scattered of me is gathered with them.
36.sharh: For him, life is nothing but living near them, when his scattered self is gathered to them again. Any other life he counts as no life at all.

translation: Whenever we are alone, we complain of love,
and our streaming tears overflow.
37.sharh: Whenever he and his beloved are alone together, each pours out to the other the pain of love, and their tears run over. Even their meetings are full of weeping, for each remembers what the separation cost.

translation: I told her of the days of our union,
a story sweet to the ear,
38.sharh: He tells her of the days when they were together, and the telling is sweet to hear. Union now survives only as a story he tells, and the story gives back a little of what union gave.

translation: and longing for that time grew
until my bed turned rough beneath me.
39.sharh: Talking of that time only made him long for it more, until his bed grew too rough to lie on and sleep left him. The poem ends at night, sleepless, where it began with the dove.

1.1.2.head: البان
1.1.2.meaning: Ban: a tall, straight tree with long fringed leaves, from whose seeds ban oil is pressed.

1.1.3.head: قُمرِيَّة
1.1.3.meaning: Qumriyya: a turtledove, a bird like the pigeon.

1.2.4.head: أَسفَع
1.2.4.meaning: Dusky: black, or black shot with red.

2.2.3.head: الطَّلَل
2.2.3.meaning: Talal: what still stands of an abandoned campsite.

3.1.2.meaning: By it: the ruin. The diwan has biha, “by her”, apparently the dove.

3.2.2.head: الخَيف
3.2.2.meaning: Al-Khayf: ground between the foot of a mountain and a watercourse; the mosque of al-Khayf at Mina, near Mecca, is named after one.

4.1.2.head: مَربَع
4.1.2.meaning: Marba': the place where a tribe camps in spring.

7.1.5.head: دِمنَة
7.1.5.meaning: Dimna: the trace of a camp, blackened by the dung and other leavings of those who camped there.

8.2.3.head: جُؤذَر
8.2.3.meaning: Ja'adhir: calves of the wild cow.

12.1.5.head: بارِق
12.1.5.meaning: Bariq: a cloud with lightning in it.

14.1.3.meaning: Su'da: a woman's name, given to the beloved.

14.2.4.head: البُرقُع
14.2.4.meaning: Burqu': a face veil worn by Bedouin women.

15.2.4.head: الأَجرَع
15.2.4.meaning: Ajra': a ridge of sand on one side and stones on the other.

16.2.2.head: الجِزع
16.2.2.meaning: Jiz': the bend of a valley.

17.2.4.head: الظّالِع
17.2.4.meaning: Limping. Two manuscripts of the diwan have al-dulla', two al-tulla'.

18.2.2.head: شُقَّة
18.2.2.meaning: Shuqqa: a long, far journey; here “their” journey (the camels') or the road to her. The diwan has shuqqatahu, the desert's long stretch.

20.1.2.head: شَأى
20.1.2.meaning: We outpace. The diwan has tash'a, “they outpace”, with the camels as subject.

20.2.4.head: لَعلَع
20.2.4.meaning: La'la': a place in the desert; a mountain, a watering place or a halt between Basra and Kufa, by different accounts.

21.2.1.head: وَجىً
21.2.1.meaning: Waja: soreness of a camel's pads from walking.

21.2.3.head: الوَخد
21.2.3.meaning: Wakhd: a camel's long, swinging stride.

21.2.4.head: اليَرمَع
21.2.4.meaning: Yarma': white stones soft enough to crumble in the hand.

22.1.4.meaning: Al-Hima: “the protected ground”, pasture closed to grazing.

22.2.1.meaning: The reciter says ahfiruha, with r. The diwan has ahfizuha, “I urge her on from behind”, which the sense needs.

24.1.2.head: طِلح
24.1.2.meaning: Tilah: camels worn out and wasted by travel.

24.1.4.head: حاجِر
24.1.4.meaning: Hajir: a place this side of the mine of al-Nuqra; the word means a bank that holds water in a valley.

25.2.4.head: الدِّرع
25.2.4.meaning: Coats of mail. The diwan has al-adhru', “forearms”.

26.1.2.head: سُعاد
26.1.2.meaning: Su'ad: a woman's name, given to the beloved.

28.1.4.meaning: “The treacherous”: the word runs over into the second half, as the meter requires.

31.2.2.head: الغانِيَة
31.2.2.meaning: Ghawani: young women admired for their beauty.

33.2.2.head: هَجَرَ
33.2.2.meaning: Shun us. The diwan has “though they shun me, or resolve to go”.

34.1.3.head: حُبّ
34.1.3.meaning: “Loving them”: being near those he loves. The diwan's text has hayyihim, “their tribe”; one manuscript has hubbihim, as here.

35.1.1.head: قَنَعَ
35.1.1.meaning: The usual form is qani'tu; the reciter says qana'tu, a form that Ibn al-Sikkit says some Arabs allowed in this sense.

36.2.3.head: شَمل
36.2.3.meaning: Shaml: all that belongs together; to have it “gathered” is to be whole again.

38.1.1.head: حَدَّثَ
38.1.1.meaning: I told her. The diwan has “I told them”.

39.2.3.meaning: Grew rough: said of a bed that will not let its sleeper rest.
